status: Provisional. Where a metric cites references, they are other projects' published figures, each measured differently. Open to discussion.

bad_pictures.label: decode errors
bad_pictures.what: Frames the client failed to decode, or decoded corrupt, on every stream.
bad_pictures.basis: Decode failures plus corrupt decodes. Any is a bug: scores 100 with none, else 0.

picture_corrupt.label: corrupt pictures
picture_corrupt.what: Decoded frames that didn't match the frame framestamp drew (its worst tile off by more than gamestream-test-client's --picture-threshold, 20 luma levels on average), on every framestamp stream: corruption the decoder didn't report, such as a picture built on a reference the client threw away.
picture_corrupt.basis: Any corrupt picture is a bug: on a clean stream the encoder's, after loss the recovery's. Scores 100 with none, else 0.

picture_recovery.label: corrupt after recovery
picture_recovery.what: The most framestamp frames in a row still corrupt from a recovery frame or keyframe on, on every framestamp stream: 0 when every recovery made the picture whole at once.
picture_recovery.basis: A recovery frame should make the picture whole. Scores 100 with none corrupt, 50 when only the recovery frame itself was, else 0.

missing_clean.label: lost frames
missing_clean.what: Frames that never reached the client's decoder on streams with nothing dropped on purpose (clean and click streams).
missing_clean.basis: Frames that never arrived on streams with nothing dropped. Scores 100 with none, 50 with up to 3, else 0.

frame_time_p99.label: frame pacing p99
frame_time_p99.what: The 99th percentile of the time between frames arriving at the client, in the frame intervals Moonshine sent at (1 is perfect pacing): each clean stream on its own, then the median stream.
frame_time_p99.basis: Gap between frame arrivals; one frame interval is perfect pacing. Rubylight reports 1.25 intervals on wired LAN, and loopback has no network to excuse more. Measured against the rate Moonshine sent at, so a game the GPU runs below the target rate isn't counted as stutter.

references.claim: arrival interval p99 20.9 ms, HEVC 1080p60, wired LAN, moonlight-common-c client

fps_delivered.label: delivered frame rate
fps_delivered.what: The share of the frames Moonshine sent that the client received on clean streams (received over received plus missing frame numbers, after the warmup): each stream on its own, averaged.
fps_delivered.basis: Frames lost or held up between Moonshine and the decoder (network, client), which frame time alone misses. A game that renders below the stream's rate isn't a delivery problem; its rate shows in host timing.

display_latency_p99.label: decoded to on screen p99
display_latency_p99.what: The 99th percentile of the time from the client decoding a frame to a display showing it, on clean streams, in the client's model of moonlight-qt presenting with V-Sync (a display at the stream's rate unless the client was given another). The model times its refreshes from where frames typically arrive, so the median is half a refresh by construction; the tail is frames queued behind late ones.
display_latency_p99.basis: The client's: its display, not Moonshine's doing. Not judged against a target; the Change column compares it with the baseline. Half a refresh is the floor; a refresh and a half or more means frames regularly waited behind a late one.

display_dropped.label: dropped by the display
display_dropped.what: Decoded frames a V-Sync display never showed, in percent, on clean streams: frames that arrived bunched, so a newer one replaced them before their refresh.
display_dropped.basis: The client's: its display, not Moonshine's doing. Not judged against a target; the Change column compares it with the baseline.

display_judder.label: judder
display_judder.what: Frames a V-Sync display showed a refresh or more later than the stream's rate needs (the frame before held on screen too long), in percent of the frames shown, on clean streams.
display_judder.basis: The client's: its display, not Moonshine's doing. Not judged against a target; the Change column compares it with the baseline.

client_decode_p99.label: client decode p99
client_decode_p99.what: The 99th percentile of the time the client took to decode a frame, in frame intervals, on clean streams. Over 1, the client decodes slower than the frames come: it's the bottleneck, and freezes and keyframes it asks for are its doing.
client_decode_p99.basis: The client's: its decoder, not Moonshine's doing. Over one frame interval the client can't keep up.

client_keyframes.label: keyframes the client caused
client_keyframes.what: Keyframes the client asked for because of itself, on every stream: its decode queue overflowed (the decoder couldn't keep up) or its decoder failed a frame. Not counted against Moonshine's RFI recovery rate.
client_keyframes.basis: The client's: none on a client that keeps up.

server_p99_ms.label: host latency p99
server_p99_ms.what: The 99th percentile of Moonshine's time on the host from capturing a frame to sending its last packet, on every stream but the packet-loss ones (their extra keyframes).
server_p99_ms.basis: Mostly the encode, which scales with resolution, not frame rate. Published figures, none a host p99: Rubylight's encode 2.6–3.1 ms at 1440p120, Punktfunk's encode p99 4.4 ms under load. The target is set from 1080p claims: at 4K the encode alone takes about 5–7 ms on RDNA 3 and 4 (henwen's 7900 XTX, rosso's 9070 XT, 2026-11-11).

references.claim: encode 2.6–3.1 ms at 1440p120 idle; mean host processing 0.45 ms on wired LAN
p50 ~0.8 ms capture to received, 720p120, NVENC zero-copy; includes the network
PyroWave encode p99 6.4 → 4.4 ms on an RTX 5070 Ti under GRID 2
4–8 ms end to end at 4K120 HDR on an RTX 4090 with encoding in the display driver, against 9–17 ms in-process (span not stated)

freeze_p95.label: recovery time p95
freeze_p95.what: The 95th percentile of how long the picture stood still after a lost frame, until a frame recovered it, in frame intervals.
freeze_p95.basis: How long the picture stands still after a loss. Recovery takes a round trip and an encode, so about three frame intervals is the floor; a keyframe takes longer.

references.claim: mean gap after a keyframe cut from 8.44 to 5.30 ms (HEVC, recovery cadence work); its "gap" isn't defined, so not comparable

recovered_without_keyframe.label: RFI recovery rate
recovered_without_keyframe.what: The share of lost frames the stream recovered from with reference frame invalidation (RFI) instead of a keyframe.
recovered_without_keyframe.basis: Losses recovered by reference frame invalidation, without a keyframe, which should make keyframes after a loss rare. Rubylight recovers 59 of 59 without one.

references.claim: AV1, 20 ms of video dropped every 1.5 s for 90 s: 59 of 59 lost frames recovered without a keyframe

click_median.label: input latency p50
click_median.what: The median time from the client sending a click to it decoding the flash the click caused (to decoded, not to photons), in frame intervals.
click_median.basis: From the injected click to the decoded flash, the whole chain but the input device and display: the app's next frame (about one interval: waiting for it, its render and the compositor's capture), then Moonshine's capture to send, the network both ways and the client's decode. At 120 fps over a LAN the last three take most of another interval, so 2 is the target.

references.claim: 5.89 ms median capture to client present, AV1 1080p60, loopback (capture to present, no input)
7 ms median picture age, capture to rendered, Retroid Pocket 6 over Wi-Fi, HEVC 1080p60 (capture to present, no input)

keyframes_per_switch.label: HDR switch keyframes
keyframes_per_switch.what: Keyframes Moonshine sent per change in the captured content's color space (SDR, HDR10, scRGB), on the streams whose content switched and that lost no frames (so no keyframe was the client asking to recover).
keyframes_per_switch.basis: SDR ↔ HDR changes the color description, which takes a keyframe; HDR10 ↔ scRGB needn't. hdrneon's cycle puts the floor at 0.67.

load_fps.label: FPS under GPU load
load_fps.what: The share of the frames Moonshine sent that the client received on clean streams with the GPU under heavy load (received over received plus missing frame numbers, after the warmup).
load_fps.basis: The slowest codec's frame rate with the GPU busy. Other hosts report 85–100% under load, and as low as 42% before fixes. Measured against what Moonshine sent, so a GPU that can't run the game at the stream's rate isn't counted; Moonshine's own rate under load shows in host timing.

references.claim: 117–120 fresh pictures/s at 120 fps under GPU load; Vibepollo 2.0 103–118 (HEVC)
a loaded NVIDIA host delivered about 25 of a game's 60 fps with 70 ms of encode latency, fixed by real-time GPU priority

peak_bitrate.label: peak bitrate
peak_bitrate.what: The busiest one-second window of bits the client received, as a share of the bitrate the stream asked for.
peak_bitrate.basis: Rate control should hold near the bitrate. Keyframes burst over it, and a link sized for the bitrate drops what doesn't fit.

unpublished.note: no published latency or pacing figures
no published latency or pacing figures
pacing features (adaptive packet pacing), no published figures

click_context.about: What a click's latency feels like next to everyday hardware. The test measures from the client injecting a click to the client finishing the decode of the flash: no input device or display (and over loopback, no network). The parts a real setup adds, and whole-chain measurements of local play and cloud streaming, come from published tests, each one setup and method; treat them as rough.

adds.claim: RTINGS' example graph: one wired mouse's clicks at about 9–11 ms, its methodology counting under 10 ms as good
